summary: Defines a YANG data model for managing the IP Traffic Flow Security additions to IKEv2 and IPsec. It lets network management tools configure and monitor these features in a standard way.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a standard settings form that lets a computer program set up and check a special privacy feature on a network device.

questions: how to configure ip traffic flow security
what does the ietf-ipsec-iptfs yang module do
how to hide traffic patterns in ipsec
subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring and monitoring IP Traffic Flow Security on IPsec tunnels.

tldr.problem: IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) improves traffic confidentiality on IPsec tunnels, but network management tools had no standard way to configure it or read its statistics.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the YANG module ietf-ipsec-iptfs, which augments the IPsec YANG models of RFC 9061 with a traffic-flow-security container for settings and with per-SA counters.
tldr.outcome: Operators can manage IP-TFS over NETCONF or RESTCONF the same way as other IPsec features, with both IKE and IKE-less models covered.

today: RFC 9348 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2023. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Module Manages
sections.content:
RFC 9348 defines a YANG module for managing the IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) extensions defined in RFC 9347. IP-TFS enhances an IPsec tunnel Security Association (SA) to give better traffic confidentiality, which makes it harder for traffic analysis to identify who is talking or to correlate observable traffic patterns.

The model follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342. It builds on the IPsec YANG modules of RFC 9061, which cover both an IKE model and an IKE-less model, and treats them as a general IPsec model to augment.
sections.plainLanguage: A special privacy mode for a network tunnel needs switches and dials. This document describes a standard control panel for those switches and dials.

sections.title: How IP-TFS Works, As the Model Sees It
sections.content:
IP-TFS uses IPsec tunnel mode to hide inner packet identifiable information, packet size and packet timing. It aggregates multiple inner packets into uniform-size outer tunnel packets, using combinations of aggregating, padding and fragmenting to fill each outer packet. Padding fills the packet when no data is available to send.

The sending side controls the behavior. Because the IP-TFS packet format is self-describing, a sender can adjust packet size and timing independently of any receiver, and each direction is independent. IP-TFS may run in only one direction, so counters for the other direction may be 0 or not updated. Any SA configured to use IP-TFS supports only IP-TFS packets, with no mixed IPsec modes.

This version of the model configures fixed-size packets sent at a constant rate, and is structured so future augmentation can add other modes. The protocol in RFC 9347 goes beyond that simple fixed mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine sending mail only in identical boxes at a steady pace, adding filler when you have little to send. Nobody watching the mail truck can tell how much real mail you have.

sections.title: The Configuration Settings
sections.content:
Under a traffic-flow-security container the module provides these settings:

  • congestion-control: a boolean that defaults to true. When true, the on-the-wire exchange needed by the congestion control algorithms of RFC 5348 is enabled. When false, IP-TFS sends fixed-size packets at a constant rate.
  • packet-size: use-path-mtu-discovery (default true) lets path MTU discovery set the maximum packet size, and outer-packet-size sets the size of the outer encapsulating tunnel packet in bytes. If the size is configured, it is only adjusted downward when path MTU discovery is on.
  • tunnel-rate: a choice of l2-fixed-rate or l3-fixed-rate, in bits per second. With congestion control on, the rate may be adjusted.
  • dont-fragment: default false. When true, inner packets too large for an outer packet are dropped instead of being fragmented across outer packets.

Receive-side and timing settings are max-aggregation-time (the longest an inner packet may be held before sending; packets that would wait longer are dropped), window-size (how many out-of-order packets the receiver will reorder; 0 disables reordering), send-immediately (default false) and lost-packet-timer-interval (how long to wait for a missing packet before treating it as lost). The two timers are in milliseconds, down to 1 nanosecond.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings say how big each box is, how fast boxes go out, whether to slow down when the road is busy, and how long the receiver waits for a late box.

sections.title: Where the Module Plugs In
sections.content:
The module is an augmentation. The writable settings are attached to the IPsec policy configuration in the IKE model, and to the policy entry in the IKE-less model. Read-only copies of the same settings are attached to the child SA information (IKE model) and to the SAD entry (IKE-less model), so a tool can read back what is actually in use.

Statistics are also read-only and are optional features: ipsec-stats provides per-SA IPsec packet counters, and iptfs-stats provides IP-TFS counters. The IP-TFS counters are split into inner-packet statistics (packets and octets sent and received, and received incomplete packets) and outer-packet statistics (all-padding and extra-padding packets and octets in each direction, plus errored and missed received packets).

These counters let an operator observe how efficiently the tunnel packets are being used.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel is bolted onto the existing IPsec panel. Some dials you can turn, and some are just gauges that show what is happening.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ipsec-iptfs in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant. It also registered the module ietf-ipsec-iptfs in the YANG Module Names registry, with prefix iptfs and reference RFC 9348.
sections.plainLanguage: The module was given an official name in the public list of names so nobody else uses the same one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH and TLS. The NETCONF Access Control Model (NACM) can limit which users may use which operations and data.

Writable data under traffic-flow-security is sensitive: writing to it without protection can harm network operations, because it decides whether IP-TFS is enabled and whether it is congestion sensitive or fixed rate.

Read access also matters. The iptfs-inner-pkt-stats and iptfs-outer-pkt-stats nodes can reveal information that IP-TFS is meant to hide, such as the true activity of the flows using it.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be allowed to change the settings, and even the gauges should be private, because they could show what the privacy feature is trying to hide.
